The comparison is with SciPy 1.18.1’s vectorised ufuncs (C/C++, one thread), measured by refbench v0.3.0 from bench/perf_test.go. The generated table is perf-table.md (data: perf.json); the public functions without a row are in perf-exempt.md.
data.method#Method: One core on both sides. refbench sets GOMAXPROCS=1 around the run and starts the SciPy worker with OMP/OPENBLAS/MKL/VECLIB_*_THREADS=1. The nd/ rows therefore run on one goroutine; the earlier multi-core column is gone. Like with like: one call over an array on both sides. Every row times one call over the same 10 000 points. The SciPy body is one ufunc call (result array allocated by the call, as the Go side allocates its own); the ufunc’s per-call overhead (about 1 µs) is amortised over the points. Three Go bodies are timed against the same SciPy call: the scalar function in a loop over the points (Gamma), the public array kernel (GammaTo: the Go counterpart of a ufunc loop, no call per element), and the nd wrapper (nd/Gamma, kernel plus allocation and dtype handling). A scalar loop calls the function once per element through a function value; SciPy’s ufunc loop does the same through a C function pointer, so that row is fair, and the kernel rows are the strict array-against-array comparison. Same bytes. The points are lo + (hi-lo)·frac(i·0.618…); go test -run TestDataParity -perf.parity compares the SHA-256 of the Go arrays with NumPy’s, row by row (all equal on 2026-11-07). Integer orders, combinatorics, reductions (bench/perf_extra_test.go). These rows carry their own Python setup, because their arguments are not all float64 arrays: Jn, Yn, In, Kn against scipy.special.jn, yn, iv, kn (orders i mod 21 as an int64 array, x in (0.1, 50); the nd/ rows pass the orders as float64, the values are the same); Factorial (non-integers, the gamma path, and a second row for integers, the table path), Factorial2, Comb, Perm against factorial, factorial2, comb, perm (Python wrappers: their call overhead is part of what SciPy costs); JnZeros against jn_zeros(2, 20); LogSumExp, Softmax, LogSoftmax over 10 000 points against logsumexp, softmax, log_softmax. go test -run TestRefSmoke -perf.smoke . runs every SciPy expression once (all run on 2026-11-08) and TestDataParity hashes the integer arrays too. LogFactorial stays exempt: SciPy has no such function. Interleaved rounds, load gate. Rounds alternate Go-first and SciPy-first; refbench refuses to time at a 1-minute load of 8 or more, and the table says deferred when no window opened. cd bench go test -run TestPerf -cpu 1 . # CI: allocations, table, inventory go test -run TestPerf -cpu 1 -perf.run . # timing (writes perf.json and the table) go test -run TestPerf -cpu 1 -perf.record . # allocation counts only
data.reading-the-table#Reading the table: A plain Go loop is faster than SciPy’s C on Gamma, LogGamma, LogBeta, Digamma, Erf, ErfInv, ErfcInv, Ndtr, Ndtri and LogNdtr (table kernels, #33), within 1.0–1.5 times on the other elementwise families, faster on the Bessel functions of order 0 and 1, on Jn and Kn and on the elliptic, zeta and polygamma functions, and several times slower where the result needs a double-double continued fraction or series (Yn, In, Iv, Kv, the incomplete beta function and its inverses, the softmax reductions). That gap is the price of results rounded correctly where SciPy’s errors run from 2 to 1e15 ulp (see accuracy.md).

data.what-was-done-33#What was done (#33): BetaIncInv/BetaIncCInv allocate nothing (#36); nd.Map2/Map3 run one direct loop for same-shape and scalar operands, bit-identical to the old path (#37). Gamma on 0 < x < 1 and x < 0 runs a float64 evaluation with an a-priori error bound and falls back to the double-double path only when the bound cannot decide the rounding, so the results are bit-identical (derivation and fallback rates: gamma-fastpath.md); sinPi/cosPi reduce their argument with an exact a - 2⌊a/2⌋ instead of math.Mod. v0.5.6: I1, I1e, K1, K1e from fitted octave interpolants (results change, more accurate); Comb by an exact integer recurrence, Factorial2 from a table, Factorial (n >= 10) and Xlog1py through certified float64 kernels, GammaSign without math.Mod (bit-identical). Not done: float64 fast paths for the remaining double-double functions. A fast path is acceptable only if a certified error bound decides when float64 is already correctly rounded, so that the bits do not move; none has been derived for the open gaps above.
